nodes.label: ecs-rds-postgres-pool Research Doc
nodes.rationale: Status is 'superseded in part' by the 2026-09-19 design spec, which settles D5/D7 and corrects C2, C5, C6 and research question 3; forward-pointers are attached at each superseded decision.

nodes.label: ecs-rds-postgres-pool Design Spec
nodes.rationale: Referenced but not included in this extraction batch; settles D5 and D7, corrects research C2/C5/C6, and is the governing spec for both plan 1 and plan 2.

nodes.label: ecs-dynamodb-rps sibling project
nodes.rationale: Repeated design reference point: the DynamoDB-based sibling project whose code, layout and measurement conventions ecs-rds-postgres-pool forks and diverges from.

nodes.label: D1: SLI stays class_threshold_ratio + availability
nodes.rationale: Pool wait is a cause, not a symptom a user feels; it gets its own dashboard row and alert rules like throttles do in the sibling, but is not made an SLO objective, avoiding a second error budget to explain.

nodes.label: D2: db.t4g.micro, autoscaling off
nodes.rationale: Reviewer instruction: 'minimal one, and use auto-scaling after to improve it' — ECS autoscaling becomes an optional third knob at the end rather than a starting condition.

nodes.label: D3: pool binds via calibrated real query cost
nodes.rationale: Calibrated on the deployed instance, not locally, targeting DBLoadRelativeToNumVCPUs ≈ 0.5 at pool_size=5 so the pool binds first while database CPU still has headroom.

nodes.label: D4: migrations and seed run on service boot behind a flag
nodes.rationale: RDS has no free gateway VPC endpoint like DynamoDB's, so migrate/seed can't run the way the sibling's deploy script does unless moved to boot time; Prisma Migrate's advisory lock makes this safe against a rolling deploy racing itself.

nodes.label: D5: second/third knob — the knob sequence
nodes.rationale: Answered 2026-09-19 with none of the three original options: instead a three-step sequence, pool_size 5→25, then desired_count 1→4 (100 connections against a ~112 ceiling), then the proxy — see design spec 'The knob sequence'.

nodes.label: D6: keep the project shape, design SQL workload on its own terms
nodes.rationale: Queries, indexes and row widths are chosen for Postgres rather than inherited from DynamoDB's cost model; accepted cost is that the two projects' results.md rows no longer share one table.

nodes.label: D7: pool wait measured via @prisma/adapter-pg + AsyncLocalStorage
nodes.rationale: Answered 2026-09-19 with option (a): options (b)/(c) rest on Prisma's $metrics feature, deprecated in 6.14.0 and removed in 7.0.0, so only owning the pool through the driver adapter and attributing waits with AsyncLocalStorage remains viable.

nodes.label: C1: making the pool the binding constraint at a generatable rate
nodes.rationale: By Little's law a pool of 5 with a 2ms query serves 2,500 qps; a naive point-select workload never binds the pool before the ALB/Fargate task does, so the calibrated cost knob must sit inside connection hold time, analogous to the sibling's pbkdf2_iterations.

nodes.label: C2: Prisma owns the pool, so there is no checkout to wrap
nodes.rationale: Superseded 2026-09-19: the section's original resolution (prisma_client_queries_wait_histogram_ms behind previewFeatures) does not exist any more, since the metrics preview feature was removed in Prisma 7.0.0; the way out is @prisma/adapter-pg with self-timed checkout (D7).

nodes.label: C3: pool wait conflates queueing with new-connection establishment
nodes.rationale: A wait measured around an await includes event-loop queueing by construction, and acquiring a brand-new physical connection (TCP+TLS+auth) lands in the same series as being queued behind other requests — opposite diagnoses in one number. Mitigated by pre-warming at boot and watching prisma_pool_connections_open / pool.total rising.

nodes.label: C4: RDS Proxy moves the wait out of the process (research Q4)
nodes.rationale: Answered yes via DatabaseConnectionsBorrowLatency et al, but the before/after comparison reads a different metric than the in-process pool.duration, and session pinning can silently turn the proxy back into a passthrough; honest pre-registered expectation against 1-4 long-lived ECS tasks is +1-2ms p95 for +$0.03/hr, i.e. likely no attainment gain.

nodes.label: C5: max_connections is a cliff (~112 on db.t4g.micro)
nodes.rationale: Reversed in part 2026-09-19: rather than designing away the ~112-connection ceiling, the spec deliberately walks toward it — desired_count=4 at pool_size=25 is exactly 100 connections, the only configuration where RDS Proxy's multiplexing mechanism is under test at all; autoscaling still stays off.

nodes.label: C6: T-class CPU credits break run-to-run comparability
nodes.rationale: Checked 2026-09-19: aws_db_instance exposes no credit_specification argument in the pinned provider (unlike aws_instance), so credit mode can't be set via Terraform; the design instead keeps db.t4g.micro and records CPUCreditBalance/CPUSurplusCreditsCharged per run, disqualifying a run that depletes the balance.

nodes.label: C7: seeded working set must fit in shared_buffers
nodes.rationale: db.t4g.micro has 1 GiB, ~a quarter for shared_buffers; exceeding it turns a 'fast' query into random gp3 reads so the first run of a day differs from the second by an order of magnitude — seed volume is a measurement parameter, not a convenience, followed by VACUUM ANALYZE.

nodes.label: C8: reaching the database at all (no free VPC endpoint)
nodes.rationale: Unlike DynamoDB's free gateway VPC endpoint, RDS needs an ENI in the VPC; three options considered (public instance + narrow SG, one-off ecs run-task seed, or migrate-on-boot) — only the public option also gives psql for debugging during a session.

nodes.label: C9: TLS and credentials only fail in AWS
nodes.rationale: RDS PostgreSQL 15+ ships rds.force_ssl=1 by default so a client working against local docker Postgres fails in the VPC unless it carries the RDS CA bundle; RDS Proxy additionally requires Secrets Manager with recovery_window_in_days=0 mandatory in a lab destroyed daily.

nodes.label: C10: new teardown survivors (RDS-specific)
nodes.rationale: Final snapshot, automated backups, the RDS log group, subnet/parameter groups, the Secrets Manager secret and the (slow-deleting) proxy are each named survivors requiring explicit guards; an RDS instance also takes 5-15 minutes to create and delete.

nodes.label: C11: comparability with the sibling project depends on route shape
nodes.rationale: If routes change shape (a SQL feed is not a DynamoDB Query) the two projects' results.md rows cannot share one table — a deliberate trade tied to decision D6.

nodes.label: C12: the SLO generator is copied, not shared, so bugs are copied
nodes.rationale: slo.yaml is per-project and generate-slo.js is duplicated rather than shared; mitigation is a header in both files naming the sibling and the fork date so a bug fixed in one is known to still be broken in the other.
